The table shows the maximum output per worker per day in two countries.
Bresk has an open economy with flexible exchange rates. Its unemployment rate is currently 3.5%, and its natural rate of unemployment is 4%. Bresk's main trading partner is Istra.

In an economy, 119 million people are employed, 5 million are unemployed, and 41 million adults are not in the labor force. Last year (the base year) the GDP deflator was 100; this year it is 110, and nominal GDP is 7,700 billion.
The required reserve ratio is 10%. A customer deposits 8,000 of currency into a checking account at First Bank. Assume banks hold no excess reserves before the deposit.

questions.stem: A shopper compares the prices of two jackets listed in dollars. Which function of money does this illustrate?

options.text: Medium of exchange
options.why: Money is being used in a different role here.

options.text: Unit of account
options.why: Correct. This matches how money is being used.

options.text: Store of value
options.why: Money is being used in a different role here.

options.text: Standard of deferred taxation
options.why: This is not one of the functions of money.

questions.explanation: Money serves as a medium of exchange (used in trades), a unit of account (measures value) and a store of value (holds purchasing power over time).

questions.stem: A savings account pays a nominal interest rate of 7%, and the inflation rate is 6%. What is the real interest rate?

options.why: Inflation is subtracted, not added.
Correct. Real rate = nominal rate − inflation.
The rates are subtracted, not multiplied.
The subtraction is reversed.

questions.explanation: Real interest rate = 7% − 6% = 1%.

questions.stem: Real GDP per capita grows at a constant 5% per year. Using the rule of 70, about how many years will it take to double?

options.text: 20 years
options.why: The rule uses 70, not 100, because of compounding.

options.text: 14 years
options.why: Correct. 70 ÷ 5.

options.text: 350 years
options.why: Divide 70 by the growth rate; do not multiply.

options.text: 10 years
options.why: This doubles the growth rate rather than finding a doubling time.

questions.explanation: Doubling time ≈ 70 ÷ growth rate = 70 ÷ 5 ≈ 14 years.

questions.stem: A natural disaster destroys a large share of the country's factories. Which of the following best describes the effect on the economy's production possibilities curve (PPC)?

options.text: The economy moves along its PPC.
options.why: Ask whether the economy's resources or technology changed (a shift) or only how fully or for what the resources are used (a movement).

options.text: The PPC shifts inward.
options.why: Correct. This matches whether resources, technology or only their use has changed.

options.text: The economy moves to a point outside its PPC.
options.why: Ask whether the economy's resources or technology changed (a shift) or only how fully or for what the resources are used (a movement).

options.text: The PPC shifts outward.
options.why: Ask whether the economy's resources or technology changed (a shift) or only how fully or for what the resources are used (a movement).

questions.explanation: Changes in the quantity or quality of resources or in technology shift the PPC. Unemployment moves the economy inside the curve; reallocating fully employed resources moves it along the curve.

questions.stem: An investor in Hollis buys government bonds issued by Aldoria. How is this transaction recorded in Aldoria's balance of payments?

options.text: Current account, as a credit
options.why: Decide whether goods or services (current account) or assets (financial account) change hands, then which way the money flows.

options.text: Financial account, as a debit (outflow)
options.why: Decide whether goods or services (current account) or assets (financial account) change hands, then which way the money flows.

options.text: Current account, as a debit
options.why: Decide whether goods or services (current account) or assets (financial account) change hands, then which way the money flows.

options.text: Financial account, as a credit (inflow)
options.why: Correct. Goods, services and income go in the current account; asset purchases in the financial account. Money flowing in is a credit.

questions.explanation: Trade in goods and services is recorded in the current account; purchases and sales of assets in the financial account. Transactions that bring money into the country are credits.

questions.stem: What is the maximum amount this bank can lend immediately?

options.why: Correct. Its excess reserves: 520 − 120.
Required reserves cannot be lent.
This is the required reserve amount.
Lending capacity comes from reserves above the requirement, not deposits minus reserves.

questions.explanation: Required reserves = 0.1 × 1,200 = 120. Excess reserves = 520 − 120 = 400, which is the most the bank can lend.

questions.stem: Bank tellers lose their jobs because customers switch to mobile banking. Which best describes this situation?

options.text: Not unemployed (not in the labor force)
options.why: Match the cause: searching (frictional), mismatched skills or declining industry (structural), or a downturn (cyclical).

options.text: Cyclical
options.why: Match the cause: searching (frictional), mismatched skills or declining industry (structural), or a downturn (cyclical).

options.text: Frictional
options.why: Match the cause: searching (frictional), mismatched skills or declining industry (structural), or a downturn (cyclical).

options.text: Structural
options.why: Correct. This matches the cause of the joblessness.

questions.explanation: Frictional unemployment comes from job search, structural from a mismatch between skills and jobs, and cyclical from recessions. People not looking for work are not in the labor force.

questions.stem: Which factor of production is a delivery truck owned by a bakery?

options.text: Entrepreneurship
options.why: Not entrepreneurship: physical capital fits this resource.

options.text: Physical capital
options.why: Correct. This matches the definition of the factor.

options.text: Land (natural resources)
options.why: Not land (natural resources): physical capital fits this resource.

options.text: Labor
options.why: Not labor: physical capital fits this resource.

questions.explanation: Land is natural resources, labor is human effort, physical capital is produced tools and equipment, and entrepreneurship organizes the others and bears risk.

questions.stem: Assume the economy is initially in long-run equilibrium. If the government increases spending on highways, what happens to the price level and real GDP in the short run?

options.text: Price level will increase; real GDP will decrease
options.why: Not this one: real GDP will increase.

options.text: Price level will increase; real GDP will increase
options.why: Correct. AD shifts right along the upward-sloping SRAS.

options.text: Price level will decrease; real GDP will decrease
options.why: Not this one: Price level will increase, and real GDP will increase.

options.text: Price level will decrease; real GDP will increase
options.why: Not this one: Price level will increase.

questions.explanation: The event changes government purchases, shifting AD right. Moving along SRAS, the price level and real GDP move in the same direction.

questions.stem: The economy has an inflationary gap. Which of the following fiscal policies would be appropriate to close it?

options.text: a purchase of government bonds by the central bank
options.why: This is monetary policy, not fiscal policy, and it moves AD the wrong way.

options.text: an increase in government purchases
options.why: This moves AD right, worsening an inflationary gap.

options.text: a decrease in personal income taxes
options.why: This moves AD right, worsening an inflationary gap.

options.text: a decrease in government purchases
options.why: Correct. Contractionary fiscal policy lowers AD.

questions.explanation: An inflationary gap calls for contractionary fiscal policy: lower government purchases or higher taxes shift AD left.

questions.stem: Which of the following is an example of an automatic stabilizer?

options.text: An increase in the reserve requirement
options.why: This is monetary policy.

options.text: The central bank buying government bonds
options.why: This is monetary policy.

options.text: Food assistance payments that rise as more households qualify
options.why: Correct. It changes with the business cycle without new legislation.

options.text: A new law cutting income tax rates to fight a recession
options.why: This requires a new decision by policymakers: it is discretionary fiscal policy.

questions.explanation: Automatic stabilizers are taxes and transfers that rise or fall automatically with income, cushioning the business cycle without new legislation.

questions.stem: As the price level falls, people need less money for transactions, interest rates fall, and investment rises. This is an explanation of the downward slope of aggregate demand known as

options.text: The exchange-rate (foreign purchases) effect
options.why: This effect works through a different channel.

options.text: The interest-rate effect
options.why: Correct. This matches the channel described.

options.text: The multiplier effect
options.why: The multiplier explains the size of AD shifts, not the slope of AD.

options.text: The wealth (real balances) effect
options.why: This effect works through a different channel.

questions.explanation: AD slopes downward because of the wealth effect (real value of assets), the interest-rate effect (money demand and investment) and the exchange-rate effect (net exports).

questions.stem: A country's current account balance is a surplus of 20 billion. Ignoring any statistical discrepancy, what is its financial account balance?

options.text: Zero, because the accounts are independent
options.why: Every payment for net imports must be financed by a net inflow of capital, so the accounts are linked.

options.text: A surplus of 20 billion
options.why: The financial account offsets the current account, so it has the opposite sign.

options.text: A deficit of 20 billion
options.why: Correct. The two accounts sum to zero.

options.text: A deficit of 40 billion
options.why: The offset is equal in size, not double.

questions.explanation: Current account + financial account = 0, so the financial account balance is -20 billion.

questions.stem: A student saves part of a paycheck to spend next year. Which function of money does this illustrate?

options.text: Medium of exchange
options.why: Money is being used in a different role here.

options.text: Unit of account
options.why: Money is being used in a different role here.

options.text: Store of value
options.why: Correct. This matches how money is being used.

options.text: Standard of deferred taxation
options.why: This is not one of the functions of money.

questions.explanation: Money serves as a medium of exchange (used in trades), a unit of account (measures value) and a store of value (holds purchasing power over time).

questions.stem: Real GDP is 500 billion below full-employment output, and the MPC is 0.8. Assuming no crowding out, what increase in government purchases would close the gap?

options.text: 125 billion
options.why: This is the tax cut that would be needed, using the tax multiplier.

options.text: 400 billion
options.why: This multiplies by the MPC; divide by the multiplier instead.

options.text: 500 billion
options.why: The multiplier means government purchases need to rise by less than the gap.

options.text: 100 billion
options.why: Correct. Divide the gap by the spending multiplier 5.

questions.explanation: Spending multiplier = 5. Required increase = 500 ÷ 5 = 100 billion.

questions.stem: What is the economy's GDP?

options.why: Imports are subtracted, not added.
Transfer payments are not purchases of goods or services, so they are excluded.
Buying stock is a financial transaction, not production.

questions.explanation: Using the expenditure approach and excluding transfers and stock purchases: GDP $$= 460 + 180 + 230 + 50 - 200 = 720$$ billion.

questions.stem: Inflation turns out to be much higher than people expected. Which of the following is most likely to be hurt?

options.text: A homeowner who took out a fixed-interest loan
options.why: This person pays fixed nominal amounts with cheaper dollars: they are helped.

options.text: A firm paying workers under a multi-year fixed-wage contract
options.why: This person pays fixed nominal amounts with cheaper dollars: they are helped.

options.text: A bank that made fixed-rate loans
options.why: Correct. They receive fixed nominal amounts that buy less than expected.

options.text: A borrower with a fixed-rate mortgage
options.why: This person pays fixed nominal amounts with cheaper dollars: they are helped.

questions.explanation: Unexpected inflation redistributes purchasing power from those who receive fixed nominal payments (lenders, savers, fixed-income earners) to those who make them (borrowers).

questions.stem: Which of the following policies is most likely to increase long-run economic growth?

options.text: A one-time tax rebate to households to boost spending
options.why: This affects aggregate demand or prices in the short run, not productive capacity.

options.text: An increase in transfer payments during a recession
options.why: This affects aggregate demand or prices in the short run, not productive capacity.

options.text: An increase in the money supply
options.why: This affects aggregate demand or prices in the short run, not productive capacity.

options.text: Tax incentives for business investment in new equipment
options.why: Correct. It increases physical capital, human capital or technology, shifting LRAS right.

questions.explanation: Long-run growth comes from more and better physical capital, human capital and technology. Policies that only change spending in the short run do not shift LRAS.

questions.stem: An economy's nominal GDP is 7,650 billion and its GDP deflator is 150. What is real GDP?

options.text: 5,100 billion
7,650 billion
options.why: Nominal and real GDP are equal only when the deflator is 100.

options.text: 7,500 billion
options.why: The deflator is an index; divide by it (over 100), do not subtract it.

options.text: 11,475 billion
options.why: This multiplies by the deflator instead of dividing.

questions.explanation: Real GDP = nominal GDP ÷ (deflator ÷ 100) = 7650 ÷ 1.5 = 5100 billion.

questions.stem: The government cuts its purchases while the central bank buys government bonds. What happens to aggregate demand and the interest rate?

options.text: Aggregate demand cannot be determined; the interest rate will decrease
options.why: Correct. Combine the effects of each policy.

options.text: Aggregate demand will decrease; the interest rate will decrease
options.why: Not this one: Aggregate demand is indeterminate here, because the two effects work in opposite directions.

options.text: Aggregate demand will increase; the interest rate will increase
options.why: Not this one: Aggregate demand is indeterminate here, because the two effects work in opposite directions, and the interest rate will decrease.

options.text: Aggregate demand will increase; the interest rate cannot be determined
options.why: Not this one: Aggregate demand is indeterminate here, because the two effects work in opposite directions, and the interest rate will decrease.

questions.explanation: Fiscal policy: AD left, interest rate down (more or less borrowing). Monetary policy: AD right, interest rate down. Where the policies agree the result is certain; where they conflict it is indeterminate.

questions.stem: The exchange rate is 8 aldos per juve. A good priced at 30 juves in Juvia is sold in Aldoria. What is its price in aldos?

options.text: 240 aldos
options.why: Correct. 30 × 8.

options.text: 38 aldos
options.why: Currency conversion multiplies by the rate; it does not add.

options.text: 3.75 aldos
options.why: Each juve is worth 8 aldos, so multiply.

options.text: 30 aldos
options.why: The price must be converted at the exchange rate.

questions.explanation: 30 juves × 8 aldos per juve = 240 aldos.

questions.stem: The central bank raises the interest rate paid on reserves. What happens to the nominal interest rate and aggregate demand in the short run?

options.text: Nominal interest rate will decrease; aggregate demand will increase
options.why: Not this one: Nominal interest rate will increase, and aggregate demand will decrease.

options.text: Nominal interest rate will increase; aggregate demand will increase
options.why: Not this one: aggregate demand will decrease.

options.text: Nominal interest rate will increase; aggregate demand will decrease
options.why: Correct. Contractionary policy raises interest rates and reduces investment.

options.text: Nominal interest rate will decrease; aggregate demand will decrease
options.why: Not this one: Nominal interest rate will increase.

questions.explanation: This is contractionary monetary policy: the money supply falls (or banks lend less), the nominal interest rate rises, investment falls, and AD shifts left.

questions.stem: Aldoria's currency, the aldo, depreciates significantly. What happens to Aldoria's net exports and aggregate demand?

options.text: Net exports will increase; aggregate demand will decrease
options.why: Not this one: aggregate demand will increase.

options.text: Net exports will increase; aggregate demand will increase
options.why: Correct. Exports become cheaper abroad and imports more expensive.

options.text: Net exports will decrease; aggregate demand will increase
options.why: Not this one: Net exports will increase.

options.text: Net exports will decrease; aggregate demand will decrease
options.why: Not this one: Net exports will increase, and aggregate demand will increase.

questions.explanation: A weaker aldo makes Aldoria's exports cheaper and imports pricier, so net exports rise and AD shifts right.

questions.stem: Assume the economy is initially in long-run equilibrium. If personal income taxes are cut, what happens to the price level and real GDP in the short run?

options.text: Price level will decrease; real GDP will decrease
options.why: Not this one: Price level will increase, and real GDP will increase.

options.text: Price level will decrease; real GDP will increase
options.why: Not this one: Price level will increase.

options.text: Price level will increase; real GDP will increase
options.why: Correct. AD shifts right along the upward-sloping SRAS.

options.text: Price level will increase; real GDP will decrease
options.why: Not this one: real GDP will increase.

questions.explanation: The event changes consumption, shifting AD right. Moving along SRAS, the price level and real GDP move in the same direction.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT included in this year's GDP?

options.text: Military equipment purchased by the government
options.why: This is a final good or service produced domestically this year, so it is counted.

options.text: Flour bought by a bakery to make bread for sale
options.why: Correct. It is excluded: a used good, transfer, financial transaction, intermediate good, non-market activity or foreign production.

options.text: A new laptop produced domestically and sold abroad
options.why: This is a final good or service produced domestically this year, so it is counted.

options.text: A new house built and sold this year
options.why: This is a final good or service produced domestically this year, so it is counted.

questions.explanation: GDP counts the market value of final goods and services produced within the country this year. It excludes used goods, intermediate goods, transfer payments, financial transactions, non-market work and production in other countries.

questions.stem: In the loanable funds market, households decide to save a larger share of their income. What happens to the real interest rate and the equilibrium quantity of loanable funds?

options.text: Real interest rate will increase; quantity of loanable funds will increase
options.why: Not this one: Real interest rate will decrease.

options.text: Real interest rate will decrease; quantity of loanable funds will decrease
options.why: Not this one: quantity of loanable funds will increase.

options.text: Real interest rate will increase; quantity of loanable funds will decrease
options.why: Not this one: Real interest rate will decrease, and quantity of loanable funds will increase.

options.text: Real interest rate will decrease; quantity of loanable funds will increase
options.why: Correct. Supply of loanable funds increases.

questions.explanation: The event shifts the supply of loanable funds right. A supply shift moves the real rate and quantity in opposite directions.

questions.stem: In the money market, the price level rises. Which of the following is true?

options.text: Money supply increases, and the nominal interest rate falls.
options.why: Check which curve the event moves, then read the new interest rate from the graph.

options.text: Money supply increases, and the nominal interest rate rises.
options.why: Check which curve the event moves, then read the new interest rate from the graph.

options.text: Money demand increases, and the nominal interest rate falls.
options.why: Check which curve the event moves, then read the new interest rate from the graph.

options.text: Money demand increases, and the nominal interest rate rises.
options.why: Correct. Changes in the price level or real GDP change how much money people want to hold.

questions.explanation: The event shifts money demand right; with the other curve fixed, the equilibrium nominal interest rate rises.

questions.stem: In a country, 92 million people are employed, 11 million are unemployed, and 110 million adults are not in the labor force. What is the labor force participation rate?

options.why: The denominator is the adult population.
Correct. $$\frac{103}{213} \times 100$$.
The labor force includes the unemployed, not only the employed.
This is the share of adults not in the labor force.

questions.explanation: Labor force = 103 million; adult population = 213 million. Participation rate = 103 ÷ 213 × 100 ≈ 48.4%.

questions.stem: A firm in Juvia exports machinery to Ferrin. How is this transaction recorded in Juvia's balance of payments?

options.text: Current account, as a debit
options.why: Decide whether goods or services (current account) or assets (financial account) change hands, then which way the money flows.

options.text: Financial account, as a debit (outflow)
options.why: Decide whether goods or services (current account) or assets (financial account) change hands, then which way the money flows.

options.text: Current account, as a credit
options.why: Correct. Goods, services and income go in the current account; asset purchases in the financial account. Money flowing in is a credit.

options.text: Financial account, as a credit (inflow)
options.why: Decide whether goods or services (current account) or assets (financial account) change hands, then which way the money flows.

questions.explanation: Trade in goods and services is recorded in the current account; purchases and sales of assets in the financial account. Transactions that bring money into the country are credits.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes the effect of the following event: the country's currency depreciates?

options.text: Long-run aggregate supply (and SRAS) shifts left.
options.why: Identify whether the event changes spending (AD), short-run costs (SRAS) or productive capacity (LRAS), then the direction.

options.text: Aggregate demand shifts right.
options.why: Correct. It changes net exports, a component of AD.

options.text: Long-run aggregate supply (and SRAS) shifts right.
options.why: Identify whether the event changes spending (AD), short-run costs (SRAS) or productive capacity (LRAS), then the direction.

options.text: Aggregate demand shifts left.
options.why: Identify whether the event changes spending (AD), short-run costs (SRAS) or productive capacity (LRAS), then the direction.

questions.explanation: The event changes net exports, so AD shifts right.

questions.stem: When disposable income rises by 500, consumption spending rises by 450. What is the value of the spending multiplier?

options.why: Correct. MPC = 450 ÷ 500 = 0.9, so the multiplier is $$\frac{1}{1 - 0.9}$$.
This is the tax multiplier in absolute value.
The multiplier is 1 ÷ MPS, not 1 ÷ MPC.
This is the MPC itself.

questions.explanation: MPC = ΔC ÷ ΔYd = 0.9; MPS = 0.1; spending multiplier = 1 ÷ MPS = 10.

questions.stem: A price index rises from 123 in one year to 139 the next year. What is the inflation rate?

options.why: This compares with the base year, not with the previous year.
This is the change in index points, not the percentage change.
Divide by the earlier year's index, not the later one.

questions.stem: A government runs persistent budget deficits financed by selling bonds to the public. Which of the following describes the likely long-run effect?

options.text: The real interest rate rises, private investment rises, and the capital stock grows faster.
options.why: Higher real interest rates make investment more expensive, so it falls.

options.text: The real interest rate rises, private investment falls, and long-run growth slows.
options.why: Correct. Government borrowing raises demand for loanable funds, crowding out private investment.

options.text: The real interest rate falls, private investment rises, and long-run growth speeds up.
options.why: Borrowing increases demand for loanable funds, raising, not lowering, the real interest rate.

options.text: The money supply increases, the nominal interest rate falls, and investment rises.
options.why: Selling bonds to the public does not create money; that would require the central bank.

questions.explanation: Deficit borrowing shifts demand for loanable funds right (or supply left), raising the real interest rate. Higher rates reduce private investment, slowing growth of the capital stock and of LRAS.

questions.stem: The government cuts its purchases while the central bank sells government bonds. What happens to aggregate demand and the interest rate?

options.text: Aggregate demand will decrease; the interest rate cannot be determined
options.why: Correct. Combine the effects of each policy.

options.text: Aggregate demand will increase; the interest rate will decrease
options.why: Not this one: Aggregate demand will decrease, and the interest rate is indeterminate here, because the two effects work in opposite directions.

options.text: Aggregate demand will decrease; the interest rate will increase
options.why: Not this one: the interest rate is indeterminate here, because the two effects work in opposite directions.

options.text: Aggregate demand will increase; the interest rate cannot be determined
options.why: Not this one: Aggregate demand will decrease.

questions.explanation: Fiscal policy: AD left, interest rate down (more or less borrowing). Monetary policy: AD left, interest rate up. Where the policies agree the result is certain; where they conflict it is indeterminate.

questions.stem: What is the price index for the current year (base year = 100)?

options.why: This is the percentage change since the base year, not the index.
Correct. Current cost 84 ÷ base cost 64 × 100.
This divides the base-year cost by the current cost: upside down.
The index weights prices by the quantities in the basket.

questions.explanation: Basket cost: base year $$6(4) + 5(8) = 64$$; current year $$6(4) + 5(12) = 84$$. Index $$= \frac{84}{64} \times 100 \approx 131.3$$.

questions.stem: The central bank lowers the required reserve ratio. What happens to the nominal interest rate and aggregate demand in the short run?

options.text: Nominal interest rate will decrease; aggregate demand will increase
options.why: Correct. Expansionary policy lowers interest rates and raises investment.

options.text: Nominal interest rate will increase; aggregate demand will decrease
options.why: Not this one: Nominal interest rate will decrease, and aggregate demand will increase.

options.text: Nominal interest rate will increase; aggregate demand will increase
options.why: Not this one: Nominal interest rate will decrease.

options.text: Nominal interest rate will decrease; aggregate demand will decrease
options.why: Not this one: aggregate demand will increase.

questions.explanation: This is expansionary monetary policy: the money supply rises (or banks lend more), the nominal interest rate falls, investment and consumption rise, and AD shifts right.

questions.stem: Real GDP per capita grows at a constant 2.5% per year. Using the rule of 70, about how many years will it take to double?

options.text: 5 years
options.why: This doubles the growth rate rather than finding a doubling time.

options.text: 28 years
options.why: Correct. 70 ÷ 2.5.

options.text: 40 years
options.why: The rule uses 70, not 100, because of compounding.

options.text: 175 years
options.why: Divide 70 by the growth rate; do not multiply.

questions.explanation: Doubling time ≈ 70 ÷ growth rate = 70 ÷ 2.5 ≈ 28 years.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes the effect of the following event: workers and firms come to expect higher inflation?

options.text: Short-run aggregate supply shifts right.
options.why: Identify whether the event changes spending (AD), short-run costs (SRAS) or productive capacity (LRAS), then the direction.

options.text: Aggregate demand shifts left.
options.why: Identify whether the event changes spending (AD), short-run costs (SRAS) or productive capacity (LRAS), then the direction.

options.text: Long-run aggregate supply (and SRAS) shifts left.
options.why: Identify whether the event changes spending (AD), short-run costs (SRAS) or productive capacity (LRAS), then the direction.

options.text: Short-run aggregate supply shifts left.
options.why: Correct. It changes production costs in the short run.

questions.explanation: The event changes input costs or expectations, shifting SRAS left.

questions.stem: At the start of the year, a government's debt is 1,000 billion. During the year it spends 330 billion (including transfers) and collects 380 billion in taxes. What is the debt at the end of the year?

options.text: 1,000 billion
options.why: The debt changes whenever the budget is not balanced.

options.text: 1,050 billion
options.why: Sign error: a deficit increases the debt and a surplus reduces it.

options.text: 950 billion
options.why: Correct. The surplus of 50 reduces the debt.

options.text: 50 billion
options.why: This is this year's deficit (or surplus), a flow, not the debt, a stock.

questions.explanation: Budget balance = taxes − spending = 380 − 330 = 50. Debt at year end = 1000 + -50 = 950 billion.

questions.stem: Potential real GDP is 2,900 billion, actual real GDP is 2,750 billion, the unemployment rate is 6.5% and the natural rate of unemployment is 5%. The economy is experiencing

options.text: long-run equilibrium at full employment
options.why: Compare actual with potential output, and the unemployment rate with the natural rate.

options.text: an inflationary gap, with unemployment below its natural rate
options.why: Compare actual with potential output, and the unemployment rate with the natural rate.

options.text: an inflationary gap, with cyclical unemployment
options.why: Compare actual with potential output, and the unemployment rate with the natural rate.

options.text: a recessionary gap, with cyclical unemployment
options.why: Correct. Output is below potential and unemployment is above the natural rate.

questions.explanation: Actual output is 150 billion below potential, and unemployment (6.5%) is above the natural rate (5%).

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes the effect of the following event: consumer confidence rises sharply?

options.text: Short-run aggregate supply shifts right.
options.why: Identify whether the event changes spending (AD), short-run costs (SRAS) or productive capacity (LRAS), then the direction.

options.text: Long-run aggregate supply (and SRAS) shifts left.
options.why: Identify whether the event changes spending (AD), short-run costs (SRAS) or productive capacity (LRAS), then the direction.

options.text: Aggregate demand shifts right.
options.why: Correct. It changes consumption, a component of AD.

options.text: Long-run aggregate supply (and SRAS) shifts right.
options.why: Identify whether the event changes spending (AD), short-run costs (SRAS) or productive capacity (LRAS), then the direction.

questions.explanation: The event changes consumption, so AD shifts right.

questions.stem: Market interest rates rise unexpectedly. Which of the following is most likely?

options.text: The fixed interest payment on existing bonds changes to match the new rate.
options.why: An existing bond's coupon payment is fixed; its price adjusts instead.

options.text: Bond prices are unaffected, because bonds pay a fixed amount.
options.why: Because the payment is fixed, the price must change for the bond to offer a competitive return.

options.text: The price of existing bonds falls.
options.why: Correct. Bond prices and interest rates move in opposite directions.

options.text: The price of existing bonds rises.
options.why: Bond prices move opposite to interest rates.

questions.explanation: When market rates rise, new bonds pay more, so buyers pay less for existing lower-paying bonds.

questions.stem: Moving from option B to option C, what is the opportunity cost of each additional unit of shoes?

options.text: $$\frac{17}{20}$$ units of shirts
options.why: This divides totals at the new option; opportunity cost uses the changes.

options.text: $$\frac{12}{5}$$ units of shirts
options.why: This divides the total shirts at the first option instead of the amount given up.

options.text: $$\frac{10}{7}$$ units of shirts
options.why: This inverts the ratio: it is shoes per unit of shirts.

options.text: $$\frac{7}{10}$$ units of shirts
options.why: Correct. 7 units of shirts are given up for 10 more units of shoes.

questions.explanation: Opportunity cost per unit of shoes = (shirts given up) ÷ (shoes gained) = 7 ÷ 10 = $$\frac{7}{10}$$. The cost rises along the table, so opportunity cost is increasing.

questions.stem: When disposable income rises by 600, consumption spending rises by 480. What is the value of the spending multiplier?

options.why: This is the tax multiplier in absolute value.
This is the MPC itself.
The multiplier is 1 ÷ MPS, not 1 ÷ MPC.
Correct. MPC = 480 ÷ 600 = 0.8, so the multiplier is $$\frac{1}{1 - 0.8}$$.

questions.explanation: MPC = ΔC ÷ ΔYd = 0.8; MPS = 0.2; spending multiplier = 1 ÷ MPS = 5.

questions.stem: At the start of the year, a government's debt is 1,000 billion. During the year it spends 460 billion (including transfers) and collects 340 billion in taxes. What is the debt at the end of the year?

options.text: 120 billion
options.why: This is this year's deficit (or surplus), a flow, not the debt, a stock.

options.text: 880 billion
options.why: Sign error: a deficit increases the debt and a surplus reduces it.

options.text: 1,000 billion
options.why: The debt changes whenever the budget is not balanced.

options.text: 1,120 billion
options.why: Correct. The deficit of 120 adds to the debt.

questions.explanation: Budget balance = taxes − spending = 340 − 460 = -120. Debt at year end = 1000 + 120 = 1120 billion.

questions.stem: An economy is in long-run equilibrium at full employment. The government permanently increases its purchases. After all adjustments, which of the following is true?

options.text: Real GDP returns to full-employment output and the price level is higher.
options.why: Correct. In the long run, output is set by LRAS; only the price level is higher.

options.text: Real GDP and the price level both return to their original levels.
options.why: AD remains higher, so the price level stays higher.

options.text: Real GDP stays permanently above full-employment output and the price level is higher.
options.why: Rising wages shift SRAS left until output returns to potential.

options.text: Unemployment stays permanently below its natural rate.
options.why: The long-run Phillips curve is vertical at the natural rate.

questions.explanation: AD shifts right, creating an inflationary gap. Nominal wages then rise, SRAS shifts left, and output returns to full employment at a higher price level.

questions.stem: If productivity rises, shifting SRAS right, which of the following best describes the effect on the Phillips curve?

options.text: A rightward (upward) shift of the short-run Phillips curve
options.why: Distinguish a movement along the SRPC (AD changes) from a shift of the SRPC (supply shocks, expected inflation).

options.text: A leftward (downward) shift of the short-run Phillips curve
options.why: Correct. Demand changes move along the SRPC; supply shocks and expected inflation shift it.

options.text: A movement down and to the right along the short-run Phillips curve
options.why: Distinguish a movement along the SRPC (AD changes) from a shift of the SRPC (supply shocks, expected inflation).

options.text: A movement up and to the left along the short-run Phillips curve
options.why: Distinguish a movement along the SRPC (AD changes) from a shift of the SRPC (supply shocks, expected inflation).

questions.explanation: Changes in AD move the economy along the SRPC (inflation and unemployment move in opposite directions). Supply shocks and changes in expected inflation shift the SRPC.

questions.stem: The government increases its purchases while the central bank sells government bonds. What happens to aggregate demand and the interest rate?

options.text: Aggregate demand will increase; the interest rate will decrease
options.why: Not this one: Aggregate demand is indeterminate here, because the two effects work in opposite directions, and the interest rate will increase.

options.text: Aggregate demand will decrease; the interest rate cannot be determined
options.why: Not this one: Aggregate demand is indeterminate here, because the two effects work in opposite directions, and the interest rate will increase.

options.text: Aggregate demand will increase; the interest rate will increase
options.why: Not this one: Aggregate demand is indeterminate here, because the two effects work in opposite directions.

options.text: Aggregate demand cannot be determined; the interest rate will increase
options.why: Correct. Combine the effects of each policy.

questions.explanation: Fiscal policy: AD right, interest rate up (more or less borrowing). Monetary policy: AD left, interest rate up. Where the policies agree the result is certain; where they conflict it is indeterminate.

questions.stem: The required reserve ratio is 10% and banks hold no excess reserves. The central bank buys 2,000 of government bonds from a commercial bank. What is the maximum possible increase in the money supply?

options.why: This is the reserve ratio times the purchase.
Correct. The whole purchase adds excess reserves of 2,000, multiplied by 10.
This ignores the money multiplier.
When the central bank buys bonds from a bank, all of the payment is new excess reserves; nothing is required against it.

questions.explanation: Buying bonds from a bank gives it 2,000 of new excess reserves. Maximum change in the money supply = 2,000 × 10 = 20,000.

questions.stem: An economy is in an inflationary gap, and the government takes no policy action. Which of the following describes the long-run adjustment?

options.text: Aggregate demand shifts left as consumers cut spending.
options.why: Self-adjustment works through wages and SRAS, not AD.

options.text: Long-run aggregate supply shifts right to meet current output.
options.why: Potential output does not adjust to the gap; the economy returns to LRAS.

options.text: Nominal wages fall, and short-run aggregate supply shifts right.
options.why: The wage change is in the wrong direction for this gap.

options.text: Nominal wages rise, and short-run aggregate supply shifts left.
options.why: Correct. Low unemployment pushes wages up, raising costs.

questions.explanation: With unemployment below the natural rate, nominal wages rise, SRAS shifts left, and output returns to potential at a higher price level.

questions.stem: Assume velocity is constant. If the money supply grows by 15% per year and real output grows by 2% per year, what is the approximate inflation rate according to the quantity theory of money?

options.why: Correct. %ΔM + %ΔV = %ΔP + %ΔY.
This is the growth rate of real output.
This ignores the growth in real output.
Real output growth absorbs part of the money growth; subtract it.

questions.explanation: With constant velocity: 15% ≈ inflation + 2%, so inflation ≈ 13%.

questions.stem: A household withdraws 400 in cash from a checking account. Which of the following is true?

options.text: M1 decreases by 400, and M2 is unchanged.
options.why: Currency, checkable and savings deposits are in M1; small time deposits are in M2 only; stocks are not money.

options.text: Both M1 and M2 are unchanged.
options.why: Correct. Check which measures each asset belongs to.

options.text: M1 is unchanged, and M2 increases by 400.
options.why: Currency, checkable and savings deposits are in M1; small time deposits are in M2 only; stocks are not money.

options.text: M1 and M2 both decrease by 400.
options.why: Currency, checkable and savings deposits are in M1; small time deposits are in M2 only; stocks are not money.

questions.explanation: M1 includes currency, checkable deposits and savings deposits. M2 adds small time deposits and retail money market funds. Moving funds within M1 changes nothing; moving from M1 to an M2-only asset lowers M1 but not M2.

questions.stem: The central bank sells government bonds on the open market. What happens to the nominal interest rate and aggregate demand in the short run?

options.text: Nominal interest rate will decrease; aggregate demand will decrease
options.why: Not this one: Nominal interest rate will increase.

options.text: Nominal interest rate will decrease; aggregate demand will increase
options.why: Not this one: Nominal interest rate will increase, and aggregate demand will decrease.

options.text: Nominal interest rate will increase; aggregate demand will increase
options.why: Not this one: aggregate demand will decrease.

options.text: Nominal interest rate will increase; aggregate demand will decrease
options.why: Correct. Contractionary policy raises interest rates and reduces investment.

questions.explanation: This is contractionary monetary policy: the money supply falls (or banks lend less), the nominal interest rate rises, investment falls, and AD shifts left.

questions.stem: Galen's currency is the gale. If incomes in Galen rise and its residents buy more imports from Delmar, what happens in the foreign exchange market for the gale?

options.text: The demand for the gale increases, and the gale depreciates.
options.why: Identify who changes their behavior, foreigners (demand) or residents (supply), and in which direction.

options.text: The demand for the gale decreases, and the gale depreciates.
options.why: Identify who changes their behavior, foreigners (demand) or residents (supply), and in which direction.

options.text: The supply of the gale decreases, and the gale appreciates.
options.why: Identify who changes their behavior, foreigners (demand) or residents (supply), and in which direction.

options.text: The supply of the gale increases, and the gale depreciates.
options.why: Correct. Foreigners demand the currency to buy its goods and assets; residents supply it to buy foreign goods and assets.

questions.explanation: Residents change their purchases, so the supply of the gale increases and the gale depreciates.

questions.stem: Which of the following terms of trade, in units of computers per unit of cars, would benefit both countries?

options.why: This is above both opportunity costs; the importer would lose.
Correct. It lies between the two opportunity costs of cars: $$\frac{10}{9}$$ and $$\frac{4}{3}$$.
Terms of trade come from opportunity costs, not total outputs.
This is below both opportunity costs; the exporter of the good would lose.

questions.explanation: Mutually beneficial terms of trade lie strictly between the countries' opportunity costs of cars, here $$\frac{10}{9}$$ and $$\frac{4}{3}$$ units of computers.

questions.stem: An economy is in a recessionary gap, and the government takes no policy action. Which of the following describes the long-run adjustment?

options.text: Nominal wages rise, and short-run aggregate supply shifts left.
options.why: The wage change is in the wrong direction for this gap.

options.text: Aggregate demand shifts right as consumers regain confidence.
options.why: Self-adjustment works through wages and SRAS, not AD.

options.text: Long-run aggregate supply shifts left to meet current output.
options.why: Potential output does not adjust to the gap; the economy returns to LRAS.

options.text: Nominal wages fall, and short-run aggregate supply shifts right.
options.why: Correct. High unemployment pushes wages down, lowering costs.

questions.explanation: With unemployment above the natural rate, nominal wages eventually fall, SRAS shifts right, and output returns to potential at a lower price level.

questions.stem: Hollis's currency, the holli, depreciates significantly. What happens to Hollis's net exports and aggregate demand?

options.text: Net exports will decrease; aggregate demand will decrease
options.why: Not this one: Net exports will increase, and aggregate demand will increase.

options.text: Net exports will decrease; aggregate demand will increase
options.why: Not this one: Net exports will increase.

options.text: Net exports will increase; aggregate demand will decrease
options.why: Not this one: aggregate demand will increase.

options.text: Net exports will increase; aggregate demand will increase
options.why: Correct. Exports become cheaper abroad and imports more expensive.

questions.explanation: A weaker holli makes Hollis's exports cheaper and imports pricier, so net exports rise and AD shifts right.

questions.stem: In a competitive market, demand increases and, at the same time, supply decreases. Which of the following describes the change in equilibrium?

options.text: Price will increase; quantity cannot be determined
options.why: Correct. Shift each curve separately: one variable moves the same way in both cases, the other depends on the sizes of the shifts.

options.text: Price cannot be determined; quantity will decrease
options.why: Not this one: Price will increase, and quantity is indeterminate here, because the two effects work in opposite directions.

options.text: Price will decrease; quantity cannot be determined
options.why: Not this one: Price will increase.

options.text: Price will increase; quantity will increase
options.why: Not this one: quantity is indeterminate here, because the two effects work in opposite directions.

questions.explanation: The demand shift alone moves price up and quantity up. The supply shift alone moves price up and quantity down. Where the effects agree the result is certain; where they conflict it is indeterminate.

questions.stem: If the price of oil rises sharply, shifting SRAS left, which of the following best describes the effect on the Phillips curve?

options.text: A leftward (downward) shift of the short-run Phillips curve
options.why: Distinguish a movement along the SRPC (AD changes) from a shift of the SRPC (supply shocks, expected inflation).

options.text: A rightward shift of the long-run Phillips curve
options.why: The LRPC shifts only when the natural rate of unemployment changes.

options.text: A movement down and to the right along the short-run Phillips curve
options.why: Distinguish a movement along the SRPC (AD changes) from a shift of the SRPC (supply shocks, expected inflation).

options.text: A rightward (upward) shift of the short-run Phillips curve
options.why: Correct. Demand changes move along the SRPC; supply shocks and expected inflation shift it.

questions.explanation: Changes in AD move the economy along the SRPC (inflation and unemployment move in opposite directions). Supply shocks and changes in expected inflation shift the SRPC.

questions.stem: The real interest rate in Hollis rises relative to the real interest rate in Istra. Which of the following is most likely?

options.text: The supply of loanable funds in Hollis decreases.
options.why: Capital inflows add to the supply of loanable funds.

options.text: Financial capital flows into Hollis, and its currency appreciates.
options.why: Correct. Investors seek higher real returns, increasing demand for the currency.

options.text: Financial capital flows into Hollis, and its currency depreciates.
options.why: Capital inflows increase demand for the currency, so it appreciates.

options.text: Financial capital flows out of Hollis, and its currency depreciates.
options.why: Higher real returns attract capital rather than repelling it.

questions.explanation: Higher real interest rates attract foreign financial investment into Hollis. Foreigners must buy Hollis's currency, so it appreciates, and the inflow adds to Hollis's supply of loanable funds.

parts.prompt: Describe a correctly labeled AD–AS graph for Bresk, showing current output (Y₁), current price level (PL₁) and full-employment output (Yf). Is the economy in a recessionary or an inflationary gap?

rubric.criterion: Labels the axes (price level, real GDP) and the AD, SRAS and LRAS curves.
rubric.example: Vertical axis: price level; horizontal axis: real GDP; downward AD, upward SRAS, vertical LRAS.

rubric.criterion: Shows short-run equilibrium right of LRAS, with Y₁ above Yf.

rubric.example: An inflationary gap, because unemployment is below the natural rate.

parts.prompt: Identify the open market operation the central bank of Bresk should use to restore full employment.

rubric.example: The central bank should sell government bonds.

parts.prompt: Describe a correctly labeled money market graph for Bresk and show the effect of the policy in part (b) on the nominal interest rate.

rubric.criterion: Labels the axes (nominal interest rate, quantity of money) with a vertical MS and downward MD.
rubric.example: Vertical axis: nominal interest rate; MS vertical; MD downward-sloping.

rubric.criterion: Shows MS shifting left and the nominal interest rate rising.
rubric.example: MS₁ to MS₂ left; i₁ to i₂ higher.

parts.prompt: Given your answer in part (c), what happens to real GDP and the price level in the short run? Explain.

rubric.criterion: Real GDP and the price level change in the correct direction.

rubric.example: A higher interest rate reduces investment and consumption, shifting AD left.

parts.prompt: How will the change in the interest rate affect the value of the brek relative to Istra's currency? Explain, and state the effect on Bresk's net exports.

rubric.criterion: Correct change in the currency's value with explanation.
rubric.example: The brek appreciates, because higher interest rates increase foreign demand for Bresk's financial assets.

parts.prompt: Calculate the unemployment rate. Show your work.

rubric.criterion: Divides the unemployed by the labor force.

parts.prompt: Calculate the labor force participation rate.

rubric.criterion: Divides the labor force by the adult population.

parts.prompt: Calculate real GDP this year, in base-year prices.

rubric.criterion: Divides nominal GDP by the deflator over 100.

parts.prompt: Some unemployed workers become discouraged and stop looking for work. What happens to the measured unemployment rate? Explain.

rubric.criterion: It falls, because discouraged workers leave the labor force and are no longer counted as unemployed.
rubric.example: Both the number unemployed and the labor force fall, and the rate decreases.

parts.prompt: By how much do First Bank's required reserves change? By how much do its excess reserves change?
What is the maximum amount by which the money supply can increase as a result of this deposit? Show your work.

rubric.criterion: Multiplies excess reserves by the money multiplier.

parts.prompt: Explain why the actual increase in the money supply is likely to be smaller.

rubric.criterion: Banks may hold excess reserves, or the public may hold some money as cash (leakages).
rubric.example: If banks keep some excess reserves or borrowers withdraw cash, less is re-deposited and lent.

parts.prompt: If instead the central bank had bought this same amount of bonds from First Bank, would the maximum increase in the money supply be larger, smaller or the same? Explain.

rubric.criterion: Larger: the whole purchase is new excess reserves and new money.
